tip: Hindi has no '-er': the adjective stays plain and से (se) marks 'than' – सोने से सस्ती (sone se sasti) = cheaper than gold, literally 'from gold cheap'.
कहीं (kahin) normally means 'somewhere' – dropped into a comparison it means 'far': कहीं सस्ती (kahin sasti) = far cheaper.
चलता हूँ (chalta hoon = I move) is the standard 'I'm off' – present tense, no future needed. फिर मिलते हैं (phir milte hain) = 'we'll meet again' = see you.
'As sweet as that' comes out as 'sweet like that': उस जैसी मीठी नहीं (us jaisi meethi nahin) = not as sweet as that one. जैसा (jaisa) = like.
होते हैं (hote hain) signals a general truth: सेब से सस्ते होते हैं (seb se saste hote hain) = are cheaper than apples, as a rule. Plain हैं would mean these bananas, today.
मिलता है (milta hai) is literally 'is gotten': सस्ता मिलता है = you get it cheaper. Hindi says where things are found cheap, not where you buy them.
सुनाना (sunana = make hear) is सुनना (sunna = hear) with 'cause' built in: बातें सुनाते हैं (baatein sunate hain) = tells us stories, literally 'makes us hear' them.
Time and measure words stay singular after a number: हर दस साल में (har das saal mein) = every ten years, with साल (saal = year) unchanged, never सालों.
ज़्यादा (zyada = more) is optional here – कल से गर्म (kal se garam) alone already means 'hotter than yesterday'. से does the comparing by itself.
पड़ता है (padta hai) is literally 'falls' – for prices it means 'works out': टैक्सी से सस्ता पड़ता है = works out cheaper than a taxi.
बुआ (bua) is specifically your father's sister – there is no generic 'aunt'. Your mother's sister is मौसी (mausi); each side of the family gets its own word.
पैर छूता हूँ (pair chhoota hoon = I touch your feet) – bending to touch an elder's feet is the deepest respect greeting, and the phrase alone works as one, even on the phone.
गाढ़ा (gaadha) is 'thick' for liquids: दही दूध से गाढ़ा (dahi doodh se gaadha) = curd is thicker than milk. A thick book or arm is मोटा (mota) instead.
अपनी (apni = one's own) always points back to the subject: प्रिया अपनी बहन से लंबी (Priya apni behen se lambi) = taller than her OWN sister. उसकी would mean another person's.
कूकर (cooker) in India means the pressure cooker – the whistling pot in every kitchen – not a stove or rice cooker.
Renting is 'taking on rent': किराए पर लेना (kiraye par lena). The thing sits 'on rent' with पर (par = on) – and renting out is किराए पर देना (dena = give).
वाला stands in for the noun: दूसरे वाले से (doosre vale se) = than the other one – no need to say होटल (hotel) twice.
Holi is played, not celebrated: होली खेलते हैं (holi khelte hain) = we play Holi. खेलना (khelna = play) is the verb for the colors and water fights.
आजकल (aajkal) means 'these days' in one word, no 'in' needed: आजकल इंटरनेट पहले से धीमा है = these days the internet is slower than before.
Elders take a plural verb out of respect: माँ stays one person but gets हैं, not है – मेरी माँ ... बनाती हैं (meri maa ... banati hain). Honorific plural marks respect, not number.
जितना (jitna = as much as) comes AFTER its noun: मिर्च जितनी तीखी नहीं (mirch jitni teekhi nahin) = not as spicy as chili – literally 'chili as-much spicy not'.
माना जाता है (mana jata hai) = 'is considered' – Hindi builds 'is done' with जाना (jana = to go): the action 'goes'. Any English 'is ...-ed' works this way.
Strong tea is कड़क (kadak = sharp, crisp) – कड़क चाय is the phrase at every stall. मज़बूत (mazboot = strong) is for walls and people, never for tea.
People are 'long', not tall: सबसे लंबा आदमी (sabse lamba aadmi) = the tallest man, using लंबा (lamba = long). ऊँचा (ooncha = high) is for buildings and hills.
से glues onto pronouns: उस + से = उससे (usse = than that one). यह कमरा उससे ठंडा है – the 'than that' is one small fused word.
बेहतर (behtar = better), from Persian, is one of Hindi's few true comparative words: पुराने वाले से बेहतर = better than the old one. Most adjectives rely on से alone.
For people, बड़ा (bada = big) means older: मुझसे दो साल बड़ा (mujhse do saal bada) = two years older than me. छोटा (chhota = small) likewise means younger.
'As well as' uses a pair: उतना ही अच्छा... जितना (utna hi achchha... jitna) = 'that much good... as much as'. Hindi spells out both halves of the match.
तेज़ (tez) covers fast, sharp, and strong: याददाश्त तेज़ (yaaddaasht tez) = a sharp memory, तेज़ चाकू = a sharp knife, तेज़ धूप = strong sun.
Verb + ने वाला makes 'the ...-ing kind': भरने वाला (bharne vala) = filling, literally 'the one that fills'. Works on nearly any verb.
This से is 'from', not 'than': छठी कक्षा से (chhathi kaksha se) = from sixth grade onward. से does both jobs; हो जाता है (ho jata hai = becomes) signals a starting point here.
Verb stem + कर = 'after ...ing': खाना खाकर (khana khakar) = after eating. Two syllables replace a whole English clause – 'having eaten, she washes up'.
Liking flips: मुझे चाय पसंद है (mujhe chai pasand hai) = 'to me tea is pleasing'. The liker takes मुझे/को (mujhe/ko = to me/to); the tea is the subject.
के हिसाब से (ke hisaab se) = 'by the account of' = according to: राजेश के हिसाब से = according to Rajesh. हिसाब (hisaab) means account or calculation.
Vehicles drink fuel: कम पेट्रोल पीती है (kam petrol peeti hai) = uses less petrol, literally 'drinks less'. पीना (peena) also covers smoking – सिगरेट पीना.
साबूदाने की खिचड़ी (sabudane ki khichdi = sago khichdi) is the classic व्रत (vrat = fast) meal – grains are avoided on fasting days, and sago isn't a grain.
Doubling a word spreads it out: अलग-अलग (alag-alag = different-different) = all kinds of. Hindi repeats where English says 'various' or 'each'.
With हमने (humne = we), the verb agrees with the thing made: बनाई (banai) is feminine because रोटी (roti) is – 'made' matches the roti, not us.
There is no word for cousin – you describe the route: मामा का बेटा (mama ka beta) = mother's brother's son. Cousins are often simply called भाई (bhai = brother).
करोड़ों (karodon = crores of): Hindi counts big numbers as लाख (lakh = 100,000) and करोड़ (crore = 10 million) – 'million' barely exists in daily speech.
मेहनत रंग लाई (mehnat rang layi) = 'the hard work brought color' – the set idiom for effort paying off. In Hindi, success shows up as color.
ही (hi) stresses the word before it: होती ही हैं (hoti hi hain) = simply ARE longer. This tiny word does what English does with voice stress or 'indeed'.
'Best in the area' becomes 'the area's best': इलाके का सबसे अच्छा डॉक्टर (ilake ka sabse achchha doctor) – Hindi reaches for का (ka = of) where English says 'in'.
बनते हैं (bante hain) = 'get made': बनना (banna) is a verb meaning 'to be made', so लड्डू बनते हैं says laddoos get made with no doer mentioned.
से can compare against an idea: उम्मीद से ज़्यादा (ummeed se zyada) = 'more than hope' = more than expected. Any noun can serve as the measuring stick.
